title: Lecture 9-18-2026
text:
Democracy
Ecnonomic Interdependance
International Institutions

Neoliberal institutionalists focus more on the roles of International Institutions in their effectiveness in guarding peace amongst liberal societies. They believe that because International Institutions reduce uncertainty, and because uncertainty increases the probability of conflict, the reduction causes by International Institutions is more effective therefore at keeping the peace.
International Institutions also reduce transactions costs. So during crisis negotiations because two states have experience negotiating through the international institutions negotiations tend to go smoother. International Institutions can also hold states accountable by providing punitive restrictions. International Institutions can also provide dispute resolution, for example arbitration through the WTO for countries that have trade conflict.




Slightly different version of Liberal Peace. When countries have financial independence they tend to remain peaceful with eachother.
The more trade between states the more peaceful those states tend to be with eachother.
Tying Hands and Sunk Cost mechanism:
If you tie your hands and make your threat credible. If I have spent too much money (sunk cost) and my hands are tied my threat is much more credible.
When a country is much more dependent on one country then when the less dependent country makes a threat it can be viewed as credible. This will lead to a higher probability of a negotiated peace or policy change.
However, the empirical finding of this situation is mixed.



Trade reduces conflict is the hypothesus, however, there is not an empirical finding that clearly backs that idea.
First, how do you measure trade dependence? - Weak Link Measure: Between State 1 and State 2, given the total trade volume between the two states divided by GDP for both countries:
$$
\frac{\text{Total Trade Volume}}{\text{GDP}_1} \lt \frac{\text{Total Trade Volume}}{\text{GDP}_2}
$$

Therefore, State 1 is the weak link because less of it's GDP comes with the trade from State 1. While State 1 may have more resources to fight, it can avoid conflict by just trading which makes it less likely to initiate conflict. 

Salience Symmetry: When neither state is particularly dependent or both are equally dependent conflict is less likely overall.
Endogeneity: Since we cannot clearly say that trade prevents or causes conflict and vice versa, Endogenity argues that with a high probability of conflict trade will reduce. Because both trade and coflict have a negative correlation with eachother, reduced trade as a result of conlfict is a side effect of conflict not a cause of it.

What instruments are good predictors of trade? These are Endogenous factors, they do not cause or are not caused by conflict but because of these factors the level of trade is predicted. So therefore, trade doesn’t predict war but the endogenous (indepdent factors) that affect trade are said to be the cause or prevention of conflict.
Endogoeous means from within, so factors from within a country that affect it’s willingness to trade with another country or have a conflict.

Trade doens’t necessarily prevent war

Opium War, War of 1812. These wars were caused directly BY trade. When the trade is unfair or unbalanceed, the country that is disadvantaged may not be willing to continue the relationship. The weaker side may be more willing to dirupt the relationship with conflict. A stronger power may try to control a weaker country via economic coercion (sanctions).
So by this logic there is correlation between trade and peace is just as strong between trade and conflict.

title: Review 10-16-2026
text:
We make 4 key assumptions:

States are rational actors
States are modeled as unitary actors
We assume the issue is always somewhat divisible
Each side has complete info

We assume that any agreement inside the bargaining range is more beneficial to both sides than an outcome achieved through war.
Let the disputed good be normalized to 1. A wins the war with probability \(P_A\), and B wins with probability \(P_B = 1 - P_A\).
Fighting costs each side something, \(C_A > 0\) and \(C_B > 0\). These costs are paid whether the side wins or loses.
Each side’s expected payoff from war is therefore
\[W_A = P_A(1) + (1 - P_A)(0) - C_A = P_A - C_A\] \[W_B = P_B(1) + (1 - P_B)(0) - C_B = 1 - P_A - C_B\]
For example, if \(P_A = 0.4\) and \(C_A = 0.1\), then \(W_A = 0.4(1) + 0.6(0) - 0.1 = 0.3\).
Because \(W_A + W_B = 1 - C_A - C_B < 1\), war destroys value. The bargaining range runs from \(P_A - C_A\) to \(P_A + C_B\), and its width is \(C_A + C_B\).
Therefore, each side is incentivized to find a settlement that falls within the bargaining range, as value gained for each side there is greater than any payoff attained through war.






This type of war occurs when another country believes another country will attack it regardless of negotiations. In such a case the country that believes it will be attacked has an incentive to strike the other country first to gain a ‘first-mover’ advantage.



When two countries have a power imbalance, when one country is becoming stronger than another rival state. That state may have an incentive to attack the country who is becoming stronger as a fight now is better than a fight when that rival state is inevtiably stronger.

title: Lecture 10-2-2026
text:
War Bargaining and Rational Actors
War Puzzle Framework

States are rational actors

They can calculate their payoffs from conflict versus other players payoffs.
These actors can make cost benefit calculations and they assume their opponents can as well.
States however, still show irrational behavior.


Let’s assume that all actors are rational, with some bound of rationality. Sometimes leaders choose to be irrational.
For example, Nixon’s mad man theory, he believed that if he dealt with the Soviet’s as a mad man it would benefit the US.

States are unitary actors.

States are black boxes
In a state there are many actors that can influence foreign policy and decision making.
In this concept however, the state is treated as a singluar actor.

Issues are subject to bargaining

Issues are assumed to be divisible, meaning that both sides can share in a positive outcome
Wars of survival challenge this assumption, as a war where one side fights for it’s survival has no positive outcome without complete victory for the surviving side.

Each State is assumed to have complete information.

We assume that war is inefficient and costly. If there is some war over a good, that war will destroy the value of that good. There is some bargaining range in which there exists some settlement outcome that doesn’t require war. If that settlement exists then why do states go to war?
States A and B are unitary rational actors. They are in dispute over some territory whose value we normalize to 1.
The value of that territory is being bargained.
State A own no portion of the territory and State B is the de-factor occupier.
In the status quo State A’s payoff is 0, and State B’s payoff is 1.
If State A’s demand is for 20% of the territory. For State B that threat is not negligible.

State A demands \(x\). Country B therefore has two options

Accept A’s demand
Reject A’s demand

Under option 1.
State A’s payoff in such a scenario is 0.4 State B’s payoff is 0.6 or 60% of the territory.
Under option 2
The two states are assumed to go to war.
Country A gets a war payout and Country B get it’s war payout \(W_A\) and \(W_B\) respectively.
Assume Country A has a 60% chance of winning.
\(Pr_A\text{win} = 0.6\) \(Pr_A\text{lose} = 0.4\)
And Country B’s probability of winning and losing
\(Pr_B\text{win} = 0.4\) \(Pr_B\text{lose} = 0.6\)
The Cost of war for the two countries is not zero.
$W_A = P_A - (1-P) (0) - C_A $
Which simplifies to
\(W_A = P - C_A\)
For State B:
\(W_B = (1-1) + P(0) - C_B\)
Simplified to
\(W_B = 1-P-C_B\)
Therefore the potential war payout for either state is:
For State A:
\(W_Z = P - C_A\)
And for State B:
\(W_B = 1-P-C_B\)
Regardless
\(1 - C_A - C_B \lt 1\)
If both states go to war neither state regardless of outcome can capture the full value of the good being bargained over. Therefore the difference in value based on the outcome of the war is considered the bargaining range or bargaining surplus
We can calculate the bargaining surplus with:
\(C_A + C_B\)
The main idea is that any agreement within this bargaining range is better than war.
Any settlement where the value of the outcome lands in the surplus from both sides means that either side benefits as the cost of war or the payoff in the event of war is less than the settlement inside the bargaining suprplus.

This logic is not universally true. Given the reservation prices of both sides, the bargaining the surplus the division of the difference in the reservation suprplus of both sides amongst them.
Negotiation can be exhausting and time consuming, so the coordination within the bargaining range may not always succeed in preventing war.
Countries payoffs from a solution within a bargaining surplus may decrease over time.
If the process of negotion becomes costly for either side their reservation price may slide and therefore it maybe more likely to accept a lesser outcome.
Ergo the side that is more patient is more likely to come up with a better outcome.

text:
Wars are said to occur because of
Issues of War:

Religion
Ideology
Economic
Trade Imbalance
Territorial
Historical Animosity

Issues of War are not the same as the reasons a state might go to war. Not all states with a trade imbalance will go to war.
Beyond Issues Based Approach to War there are a few other opinions as to why war occurs:

Leaders are sometimes or always irrational and do not respect the cost of war.
Leaders who order war enjoy the benefits of war but struggle to see the costs of war.
Even rational leaders who consider the costs and risks of war may still end up fighting nonetheless

These are the 3 common arguments as to why leaders choose to war. The reason as to why leaders choose to go to war is called the The War Puzzle.
The third reason is called the Rationalist Explanation of War

State B must consider whether to accept or reject the demand.
State A could maintain the status quo, or it could make the threat with the demand that State B give up X (20% control of the disputed territory).
If State B agrees with State A’s demand both countries can reach an agreement.
Considering, the agreement, Country A’s payoff would be the territory gained via the negotiation.
Country A’s payoff in such a scenario is X And Country B 1-X

 = P = 1-P 
C_A C_B $$
The Cost of War is always Postive
\[
0 \lt C_A

\]
Bargaining Range Surplus is Said to Equal C_A + C_B
The total cost of war is the total amount of resources that both states must give up in order to go to war. If both states reach a negotiated settlement it’s always better for both countries.

Therefore, looking at the table it’s easy to find that when a democracy initiates a war it is less likely to lose. It’s also possible to see that in general democracies tend to not get involved in wars. Even when being targeted, democracies tend to win more than they lose.
Under which \(X^2(6) = 12.7, p - 0.48\) indicating that the differences in the table are statistically significant.
These wars are all wars with more casualties than 1000 since 1816. Anocracies are a mix of a democracy and an autocracy.
In 1992 David Lake found that democracies win more often than lose in warfighting. The major work was done by Reiter and Stam (2002) and they distinguished two clear mechanisms:
In terms of duration of wars, democracies tend to have wars of shorter lengths than that of Anoncracy and Autocracy. Democracies also tend to have lesser casualties.


In democracies political leaders tend to want to maintain their political offices, fighting a losing war is a really good way to lose your office, therefore, democratic leaders tend to choose wars they can win.
Democracies tend to initiate conflicts against targets that are inferior, as opposed to autocracies that will initiate wars against inferior targets. This is called the Selection Mechanism
When democratic leaders lose a war they are very likely to lose their office. THis mechanism is based on the selctorate theory. Democracies are not inherently better warfighters, however, they tend to select particular kinds of wars they are more likely to win.
When you compare the combatants of the above table, democratic war powers have drastically more resources and power than their opposing belligerents. Despite this, autocratic leaders tend to face harsher consequences when losing wars as the result of them losing office tends to be more severe in nature.
Democracies are more willing and more able to mobilize resources, once committed, democratic resources tend to overwhelm autocracies. When autocracies and democratic leaders started wars (in war games) with identical resources, 2/3 of the time democratic leaders outspent autocratic opponents. Reiter and Stam argue that democratic societies are more open and are able to be more innovative and have a more transparent and therefore effective communication which provides better logistics, leadership, and initiative.
Overall, democracies (democratic peace) tend to not fight against eachother. Democratic societies tend to fight harder but also tend to select wars that are easier to win. Democracies also tend to fight shorter wars. As wars drag on, democratic societies tend to lose their initiative whereas autocratic societies tend to be able to fight harder for longer. When a democratic war drags on, it may become the political high ground to stop fighting the war.

title: Lecture 10-12-2026
text:
Leaders have an incentive to iniate conflict to divert attention from domestic problems.
Therefore domestic weakness can increase conflict. This can lead leaders to “play tough”.


If an opposing state knows that because of domestic weakness a leader is playing tough, the opposing state is incentivized to avoid conflict with that state.
Therefore domestic weakenss can serve as bargaining leverage. But some others argue that it actually leads to vulnerabilities in terms of international bargaining. So which is it?
According to the Diversionary Conflict Theory the leader who is weak domestically has a more credible threat.

Tying Hands Mechanism Similarity
If a popular leader backs down from a threat while he’s popular, he’s going to to pay an audience cost. Popular leaders have some audience cost cushion whereas unpopular leaders do not.

title: Lecture 10-12-2026
text:
Win Sets and Ratifications
A win set is a set of possible international agreements that can obtain domestic approval. The overlap between the win sets of the negotiating states determines whether a mutually ratifiable bargain exists.
When two countries have large win sets, then it it likely they will be able to come to an agreement, this however, reduces leverage because both parties know that each side has room to concede.
With a small win set, this makes coming to an agreement harder. Likewise a smaller win set means that a country has less incentive to give leeway to the opposing negotiation.

title: Lecture 10-12-2026
text:
Determinants of Win Set Size

Domestic preferences and coalitions: A wide distribution of acceptable outcomes can enlarge the win set. Deep polarization or powerful veto groups have the ability to shrink the size.
Political Institutions: Ratification rules, legilatures, courts, coalition governements, etc. all affect the size of the win set.

title: Lecture 10-12-2026
text:
Bargaining Implications & Strategy

title: Lecture 9-9-2026
text:
Balance of Power Theory and power-transition theory are both systemic theories, they explain war and peace with reference to the overall distribution of power across the system.



Disparty in power between major powers can make states feel insecure.
Power imbalance is treated as a paossible cause of war, and bipolarity is presented as potentially producting greater stability.
The balance-of-power tradition developed in multipolar systems where states sought to prevent the emergence of a hegemonic power.
Alliance formation is one method of balancing power.
A fundamental assumption is that states seek power because of security concerns in a self-help system.





Parity in power between major powers can create insecurity, so power balance is treated as a more probable cause of war.
Power preponderance can produce a more peacful international system, with implications at both the dyadic and systemic levels.
The direct cause of systemic instability is a shift in power between a rising challenger and a dominant status-quo power.

So in one theory (Balance of Power) two major powers with equal power creates a stable political system, whereas Power Transition Theory states that a single hegemon creates a stable system and countries rising in power create a higher likleihood of conflict.




Anarchy means the lack of a central authority capable of dictating and enforcing the legitimate use of force above sovereign states.
Anarchy does not mean chaos or complete abscense of order, international orders can and do exist.
Even realist theories recognize that mechanisms such as the balance of power can create forms of international order.
Anarchy differentiates international politics from domestic politics, where hierarchical enforcement mechanisms normally exist.





Soereignty implies that there are no de jure or de factor enforcement mechanisms reliably superior to states in all matters of security.
In a self-help system, states ultimately defend themselves through their own capabilites rather than relying completely on external protection.
Even when states would prefer mutual restrait such as complete disarmament, each state faces uncertainty about whether the other will remain commited.





A state’s attempt at self-defense may involve military build up.
Other states cannot be certain whether the increased military power is purely defensive.
Even a defensive buildup can therefore increase the security concerns of rivals or opponents.
Fear of exploitation creates a cooperation versus defection problem.
An arms race is a natural outcome of this dilemma.

Morgenthau’s Six Principles of Classical Realism

Politics is governed by objective laws rooted in human nature.
Interest is defined in terms of power.
Interest defined as power is unversally valid and constate, althought the meaning and forms of power may change.
The moral significance of political actions must be considered in the context of political consequences.
There is no universially agreed set of moral principals among states.
The political sphere is autonomous from legal, moral, or economic spheres, politics should be studied on it’s own terms rather than governed by legal or moral guidelines.

title: Lecture 10-9-2026
text:
Why Leaders Go To War (Cont.)

In-Out-Group Mechanism

Only works when the group is small and has a pre-existing cohesion.
If a society is already highly bipolar then these hypothesus are not likely to hold.

Rally Effects

These effects are small and short lived
E.g. in previous lecture Argentinian president popularity during Falklands War.
In some cases there are exceptions like Winston Churcill during WWII, but that required a massive external threat.
George Bush’s initial victory in Iraq gave him a boost but that boost was so small it did not even help him achieve re-election.
Another criticism of this mechanism is that the public is not naive, they question why leaders go to war, they realize that leaders may initiate wars because they are desperate for popularity.
The positive effects of rallying are smaller just before elections.

Scapegoat mechanism

The ability to blame domestic problems on external threats
It’s hard to associate all domestic issues with external threats.

Gambling of Resurrection

This can be argued to be the worst position a leader can be in. For a leader to want to gamble on starting a war to potentially win re-election is a very desperate mechanism. This mechanism does not in many ways help a leader in terms of gaining electoral victory.
Costly wars can also inflict punishment and further negative outcomes rather than a higher chance of re-election.


Each of these four mechanisms have significant shortcomings and lack significant empirical findings.
Empirical Tests for Diversionary Mechanism
In order to test for this there must be specific domestic patterns: 1. Low Leader Approval 2. Economic Crisis With those issues in place studies look at the correlation between those domestic issues and a state’s propensity to go to war.
Studies have found that there is positive correlation between states experiencing these issues and therefore can said to prove to some degree that there is evidence of diversionary theory.
These problems cannot be said to cause conflict or war, meaning that it is difficult to cause causation between those domestic patterns and the probability of a state to initate/engage in conflict.
Many of these studies have focused on the United States because approval ratings on US presidents are widely available. The US is also one of the only states that can freely initiate conflict without significant costs. This is called major power bias. There was strong evidence with regards to the US in terms of domestic conflicts and positive correlation with external conflict. But when smaller powers like the UK or Israel were studied the same evidence was not found.

Strategic Conflict Avoidance

Targets of conflict tend to avoid conflicts against unpopular leaders because they know they have some incentive to engage in conflict. By this logic other countries should be less likely to go to war against the US during election periods. The enemy would want to avoid the rally affects of attacking a state.
Wars that the US has fought in tend to be initiated early on during a US president’s tenure, not near election periods.
In the US the president enjoys a ‘honeymoon period’ where the presidents approval rating is positive early on during his term. (Usually around the first six months). Most conflicts or war occur during the early period. The enemy specifically does not want to provide any political benefit to the US. This supports the logic of strategic conflict avoidance.
But this means that if you are an unpopular leader and you know the enemy would want to avoid conflict this means you could theoretically levy huge demands. The target therefore would want to avoid conflict but this is where the theory breaks down as to some degree super unreasonable demands could still incentivize the opposing nation to want to engage in conflict.

title: Lecture 9-14-2026
text:
Democracies are not inherently more peacful towards autocracies.
Democracies tend to be more peaceful towards other democracies. However, democracies are as likely as autocracies to initate interstate conflicts.
Diatic Democratic Peace: Democracies are more peacful to eachother but just as violent as other political systems when not dealing with other democracies.


Democratic norms tend to have less human rights violations, and they tend to be lesser in severity when compared to autocracy. Autocracies are more likely to use violence to resolve domestic disputes.
Key Assumptions*

Externalization:
Institutionalization: Selectorate Theory - The fundamental difference between autocratic and democractic societies is the size of winning coalition. When multiple people have a say in domestic politics are called the selectorate. The support of the selectorate for a leader is not necessary for their political survival, for example you want people to support your party when you exit office so they will elect your party. The same applies to autocracies, in fact it’s more severe there because their literal survival is on the line if they lose power.

In order for leaders to accomplish their survival they must understand whose support is necessary for survival. Support of the entire selectorate tends to not be neccesary, the members whose support is necessary for the survival of the leader is considered the “winning coalition”. For example in an autocracy this “winning coalition” might be just the military leadership, etc.
In a democracy the winning coalition tends to be much larger than that of the winning coalition in an autocracy. In a democractic society the winning coalition tends to be broad public support.
Autocratic leaders tend to use private goods to entice military leadership to support their regime. Private goods are like patronage goods, they are given only to a small group of peoples.
In democratic societies, leaders tend to win broad public support (or support of their winning coalition) via the provision to the general public of public goods. Public goods tend to be more effecient at capturing winning coalition than private goods because it can grab larger support than the scarce private goods.
Assumption War Outcomes are a public good. Meaning a democratic leader must win active wars in order to survive as a leader. Therefore, democratic leaders tend to be very cautious in selecting when to engage in wars, and when they do engage in war they tend to select easier opponents to ensure positive outcomes in wartime. In autocracies, leaders have a lesser incentive to see positive outcomes in wars and therefore autocracies tend to have more wreckless foreign policy.

However this outcome could be argued to be wrong because in a democratic society the outcome of a war tends not to benefit the totality of the winning coalition, instead it behaves more like a private good because it benefits a select few while still imposing costs on the broad public.


Constraints Persepective: Regardless of regime type, many people do not want to pay the huge cost of war. Democratic leaders have to pay more attention to public support/aversion to any given conflict. This plays heavily into their decision to decide to fight a war or not.
Democracies are more transparent than autocracies. Information is more freely available in democracies. Economic data published by China is less trusworthy. War and conflict is more likely when there is large uncertainty. When democracies are in crisis there tends to be less uncertainty, which means less conflict. Democracies have more informational advantages which means they are more certain and therefore much less likely to engage in conflict. When democracies make threats therefore, they tend to be more credible. When democratic leaders make a public announcement or a threat, it is politically costly, this is called audience talk, because the threat ties to democratic leaders hands with his winning coalition, the democratic leaders more likely to follow through because he will pay a much higher political cost. If the democratic leader doesn’t follow through he pays a high audience cost.
Democratic citizens do not want to fight against other democracies. Democratic public opinion has a strong sway on democratic leaders to prevent war against other democracies.
Socialization: If you are brought up in a system where it is not normal to use force or violence against opposition, you will tend not to use, the same could be inversely said about those raised under autocratic systems. This explanations shortcoming is that it points more to a monotonic democratic peace, but this peace lacks empirical evidence.

title: Lecture 8-31-2026
text:
Reference Notes

State, Sovereignty
There is no higher power above the state within it’s own territory. Each state should be allowed to dictate it’s own behavior. No international actor should be allowed to dictate a state’s behavior. This is the concept of Sovereignty.
Anarchy is the absecene of supra-national authority. There is no enforcement mechanism other than the soverignty of the state.
The treaty of Westphalia (1648) is considered as the reference point for the idea of the modern state or when state sovereignty was first recognized.
A State is a formal legal system with a central authority that makes and enforces it rules within a defined territory.
A nation is a cultural group of people and it not recognized as an international actor.
Nation-State is a state that shares within itself a unified social and cultural identity.
Country is a common term to refer to a geographic area of a state.
Extra-Systemic Conflict: When a state fights against a non-state actor.

US achieved internal sovreighty by declaring itself indepdent in 1776, but it lacked external sovreighty (it wasn’t recognized by external states). But in 1781 when the Treaty of Paris was signed the US gained external sovreighty.
Autonomous Territories look like states but are not actually states, e.g. Greenland.

title: Lecture 10-5-2026
text:
States are rational actors, typically a state is a collective actor. But in International relations they are considered unitary actors.

States can exhibit irrational behavior, especially when the state is ruled by the preference of just a few elites.

Any given issue in emergency bargaining is divisible which lends space for negotiation.
Each State has complete information.

Under these assumptions the war puzzle both have some cost of war that prevent either state from achieving a perfect outcome. Therefore, the bettter outcome is always a negotiated settlement that lands in the range of the “Bargaining Surplus.”
Any agreement in the bargaining range explicitly allows the countries war payoff (really payoff inspite of war) to be greater than had they fought that war and won.

All of these cases present that there is some uncertainty that causes countries to miscalculate and go to war.


Between two states bargaining State A and State B have some information that is prviate to them. This information is something they would want to misrepresent to the opposite state.
E.g. China and the US negotating a slow down to the AI arms race.
IF the US or China knows exactly where the US’s reservation price is at its lowest, China will always demand that value. So therefore, the US must present misinformation in order to force China to choose an ambiguous reservation price, or the price they believe that the US is willing to settle on. Tying Hands
When a democratic leader makes a threat and backs down, they will pay a much higher audience cost than an autocratic leader who does the same thing.
Therefore, when a leader of a democractic country makes a threat, it is typically much more credible because the cost of that threat is potentially much higher for a democratic leader.

title: Review 10-16-2026
text:
Win-Sets
A set of agreements that both international leaders and their respective domestic audiences will ratify.
Where both the international leaders agree and their domestic audiences would ratify those agreements, those are called domestic win-sets.
When a country has a large amount of win-sets they are said to have less leverage in negotiations as the other country may understand that they will have space to make concessions.
Likewise a state with a small win-set, they are more likely to negotiate without making much concessions because there is a small amount of outcomes that their domestic audience will support. Therefore, that increases a leaders bargaining leverage.
